title: Lazy nested-list iterator
prompt:
Build an iterator that walks an arbitrarily nested list of integers and yields the integers in left-to-right order, one at a time, without flattening it up front.

- Implement the class NestedIterator(nested) with next() and hasNext() (has_next in Python). The driver runNestedIterator(nested, ops) is already written: ops is a list of "next" / "hasNext" strings and it returns one output per op (the integer, or true/false).
- nested is a list whose items are integers or lists of the same shape. Lists may be empty, and nesting can be up to 1,000 levels deep, so avoid recursion.
- next is only called when hasNext would return true. Up to 100,000 integers in total.
- Do not build a fully flattened copy in the constructor: extra memory should be proportional to the nesting depth, not the number of integers.
hints: A recursive walk is easy, but an iterator must pause between values. What does the recursion remember while it is paused?
Keep an explicit stack of (list, index) frames, one for each level you are currently inside.

In hasNext, loop: pop frames whose index reached the end; if the current item is a list, advance the index and push a frame for that list; stop when the current item is an integer. next calls hasNext, then returns that integer and advances the index.

solution.explanation: The stack holds one (list, index) frame per open level of nesting, which is exactly what a recursive walk would keep on the call stack. hasNext advances until the top frame points at an integer: it pops finished lists and descends into sublists, so empty lists are skipped naturally. next calls hasNext and then returns the integer and moves that frame forward.

complexity.notes: d is the maximum nesting depth. Each list is pushed and popped once, so the total work over a full iteration is linear in the size of the structure.

followUps: Add a peek() method that returns the next integer without consuming it.
How would you iterate in reverse (right to left) with the same memory bound?
